nameStory: Devil's-bit scabious gets its intriguing name from its peculiar root, which appears to have been bitten off or truncated at the end. Medieval folklore claimed that the devil bit off the root in anger because the plant was so useful for healing that it interfered with his evil work. The name 'scabious' comes from the Latin word for 'scab,' as these plants were traditionally used to treat skin ailments.
description: Devil's-bit scabious is a charming perennial wildflower that produces rounded, pincushion-like flower heads in shades of blue to purple. Growing 1-3 feet tall, it forms neat clumps with simple, oval leaves arranged in pairs up the stem. The distinctive flowers sit atop slender stems like small powder puffs, making them easy to spot in late summer meadows. This European native is extremely rare in New England, with only a handful of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Rounded, dome-shaped flower heads about the size of a large marble, composed of dozens of tiny blue-purple flowers packed tightly together like a pincushion. Each individual flower has four petals and extends slightly beyond the flower head, giving it a fuzzy, soft appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple, oval to lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. The leaves feel smooth and somewhat succulent, with prominent veining and no teeth along the edges. Basal leaves form a neat rosette.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms compact clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple upright stems. Each stem typically supports a single flower head at its tip, creating an orderly, almost garden-like appearance even in wild settings.

idTips.label: Root
idTips.description: The root appears abruptly cut off or truncated, as if someone took a bite out of it. This distinctive 'bitten' appearance is unique and gives the plant its memorable common name.

habitat: In its native range, devil's-bit scabious thrives in nutrient-poor, damp grasslands, heathlands, and limestone or chalk soils. In New England, the few documented populations have been found in managed meadows or naturalized areas, likely escaped from cultivation or introduced accidentally.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in neat basal rosettes, with fresh green growth appearing smooth and succulent-like.
seasonality.summer: Flower stems elongate through mid-summer, with the distinctive rounded flower heads blooming from late July through September.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and produce small seeds, while leaves may remain green well into autumn in mild conditions.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving only the distinctive truncated root system underground.

funFact: This plant was so highly valued in medieval times for treating plague and other ailments that people believed the devil himself was jealous enough to bite off part of its healing root - which is why the root really does look like something took a bite out of it!
confusionNotes: The rounded, pincushion-like flower heads might be confused with native wild bergamot or button bush, but devil's-bit has much smaller, more compact flower heads and completely different leaf arrangement. Its opposite, simple leaves and European origin help distinguish it from most native look-alikes.
contextualKnowledge: Devil's-bit scabious is extraordinarily rare in New England and should be reported if found, as it may represent escaped garden plants or new introductions. It's sometimes grown in wildflower gardens for its attractive late-season blooms, which is likely how it occasionally appears in the wild here.
compareHints: As the only Succisa species in New England, devil's-bit is most similar to other members of the honeysuckle family like teasels or field scabious. However, it differs from teasels by having much softer, rounded flower heads rather than spiky ones, and from field scabious by its simpler, undivided leaves and more compact growth habit.
